answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
In general, the main challenge lies in determining the marginal electricity that will be replaced by a new project. Even over short time horizons (e.g., tomorrow or next month), identifying the marginal electricity on an hourly basis is complex to determine (weather, load etc.). Extending this assessment to a 20–30‑year timeframe appears highly unrealistic. Such an exercise would include estimating the consumption / load in the future, the existing composition of power plants, prices for fuel and finally the market penetration of emerging technologies such as hydrogen powered gas power plants, large scale battery storage etc.
Overall, the attempt to calculate the consequential impact may lead to arbitrary outcomes, given the difficulty of determining a large number of variables and their interdependencies, combined with the inherently subjective selection of the marginal electricity assumed to be displaced. It is also unclear how a harmonised accounting and selection of the marginal electricity will be guaranteed across different practitioners.
Finally, there is the risk that the term "consequential" could be associated with Consequential LCA: if the present proposed methodology is not in line with the requirements of consequential LCA (e.g. indirect land use changes, influence of changing fuel prices by fuel switch on other potential consumers etc.), it would be advisable to make a clear disclaimer outlining the differences.

answers.label: Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: A more detailed explanation would be required for a thorough review, as several methodological aspects in the formula remain insufficiently defined. Additional clarification would significantly improve the ability of practitioners to assess the proposed approach and evaluate its practical implications.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
Although the impacts of infrastructure are usually limited for fossil-based electricity generation, they represent dominant share of the overall impacts for certain renewable technologies - such as photovoltaic and wind power. This includes also, for example, GHG emissions associated with the production, construction, installation, and, where applicable, fuel supply chains for technologies such as nuclear or biomass.
An inclusion of these elements would be therefore recommended although such an expansion would primarily affect Scope 3. A similar consideration might be relevant for consequential impacts such as indirect land use changes that might be associated to new projects. From pragmatic perspective, incorporating those aspects would further increase the complexity of the impact calculation.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
Given the substantial challenge associated with determining the marginal impact of a new project on an hourly basis over its entire lifetime, conducting an annual calculation—or at minimum an annual review of the initial assumptions and calculations—is strongly recommended.
Furthermore, within the annual reporting process, it would be advisable to distinguish infrastructure‑related impacts from marginal impacts, recognising that infrastructure‑related impacts do not require annual reporting once the project is operational.
However, in order to a comprehensive response to Question 24, the overall objective of the methodology requires clearer articulation. In particular, it would be important to specify the intended users (e.g., corporate reporters, project developers, policymakers) and the purpose of the reporting—whether it is intended to support carbon credit generation, regulatory claims, or voluntary disclosures.
Finally, it would be recommended to specify what are the advantages of annual reporting of consequential accounting, in parallel with the Scope 2 attributional accounting - while explicitly noticing that companies are not permitted to report "avoided emissions" alongside their Scope 2 emissions.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text:
The information provided for the different methods is insufficient to enable meaningful feedback on their appropriateness. Overall, there is a significant likelihood that determining marginal emission rates at an hourly resolution cannot be achieved using the proposed approaches. This challenge is strongly influenced by the selected reporting timeframe, as noted in response to Questions 24 and 25.
From an energy‑sector perspective, it appears unlikely that the proposed methods or models would be capable of generating ex‑ante marginal emission rates for the entire lifetime of a project. For an ex‑ante annual calculation, methodologies such as the “heat‑rate/LMP” or “statistical” approaches may be feasible; however, the challenges previously described (see response to Question 18) could still result in arbitrary assumptions for specific hours.
Finally, an important consideration concerns the responsibility for generating marginal emission rates and the underlying data for a given grid, sub‑grid, or region, as well as the entity responsible for ensuring data quality and methodological consistency.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text:
Methodologies that may be appropriate: "Policy scenarios" as it is the least based on assumptions, as well as "Capacity expansion modeling", which is only as reliable as the model it is based on.
Methodologies that may not be appropriate: "Recent capacity additions" as well as "Average emissions rate" as they extrapolate the past into the future, which is always debatable for long time horizons.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text: Through a case study, by applying the different methods for different situations (market with high incremental electricity demand, market in transformation from fossil to renewable, generation projects with different levels of intermittency).

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text: The emission impact of a new project is likely not the primary challenge; rather, the key issue is the estimated reduction relative to the generation that is displaced. As the projection horizon extends further into the future, the associated uncertainty will inevitably increase, and the effort required to provide information at an hourly level of granularity would become substantial.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text:
Country or regione. The response provided in the previous question is intended to reduce the effort required to the methodology's intended users, recognising that the required effort increases substantially as the level of granularity becomes more detailed.
However, there is a dependency on the geographical location the new project is implemented, as well as a temporal dependency, especially in cases where marginal power is based on renewable. A broader discussion is needed on the trade‑off between what is feasible and what is both accurate and meaningful. For example, in contexts with high share of renewables, such as Germany, a wind project may, at certain hours, effectively displace other wind generation. In such cases, an hourly resolution becomes essential to avoid misleading conclusions. As renewable penetration increases, determining the true marginal power source becomes progressively more complex.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text:
Annual resolution is the more pragmatic approach; however, there are dependencies as specified in the response to question 44.
An accurate consequential calculation would probably require an hourly resolution, due to the fact that generation from e.g. PV or wind have a high intermittency. However, the effort required for the calculation would be high and it is also uncertain whether this information is publicly available.
It would be advisable to provide further elaboration on the necessary temporal and spatial granularity. In addition, clarification would be beneficial regarding how this information will be made accessible to companies seeking to calculate consequential impacts.

answers.label: Why selected weighting approaches are appropriate
answers.text: It would be valuable to understand how build‑margin and operating‑margin emission rates differ across relevant scenarios, as well as to assess the robustness of these values. If the associated uncertainty is inherently high, the weighting between the two metrics becomes not relevant anymore.

audit_basis: Supplies life-cycle and ESG software and datasets alongside advisory work; Q37 argues about who should generate and quality-assure marginal emission rate data.
